title: Does this shape of six squares fold into a cube?
description: Six squares are joined as a row of four, one above the first and one beside that. The board folds the row into walls, then the other two squares, and checks each face of the cube. Keeko's doubt is that six squares are always enough.
teaching_notes: One idea: fold in the mind and check that each of the six squares lands on a different face. Watch for students who say a shape of six squares always folds into a cube.

source: Six squares: a row of four, one square above the first squar
video_script.why: The child tests a shape of six squares by folding it in the mind, because a net needs every face covered once and no face covered twice.
video_script.substitution: row of four folds into four walls; the square above the front is the lid; the square left of the lid lands on the left wall again.
video_script.anchor: the shape of six joined squares from the book, folded on the stage
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says six squares are enough because a cube has six faces; but two squares land on the same face and the bottom stays open, so the doubt is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: No, it is not a net of a cube

final_answer.value: No, it is not a net of a cube
final_answer.spoken: no, it is not a net of a cube

hold_back: No, it is not a net of a cube
maths_rules: shape: row of 4 squares R1 R2 R3 R4, one square T above R1, one square S to the left of T
the row of 4 folds round into 4 walls; R1 is the front; the left wall beside R1 is R4
T is joined to the top edge of R1, so T folds over as the lid
S is joined to the left edge of T, so S folds down onto the left wall, where R4 already is
left wall covered twice and the bottom covered by none: not a net of a cube
video_script.design: One idea: fold in the mind and count the faces. The shape folds on the stage; the doubled wall and the empty bottom glow in the warning colour.
